ex01: Start with an empty array and loop from 1 up to and including n.
Reuse your FizzBuzz logic from module 02 for each number, and push the result into the array.
Check divisibility by both 3 and 5 first, and remember to push numbers as strings.
ex02: Split the sentence into words, transform each word, then join them back with spaces.
Each word is its first character in uppercase followed by the rest of the word in lowercase.
charAt(0) on an empty string returns an empty string instead of undefined, which keeps the empty case working.
ex03: First build a clean version of the text: lowercase, with only letters and digits.
Once the text is clean, compare it with its reversed version.
To reverse a string, you can split it into characters, reverse the array and join it again.
ex04: Two words are anagrams if, after sorting their letters, they become exactly the same string.
Lowercase both words and remove the spaces before comparing.
Another way: count how many times each letter appears in each word and compare the counts.
ex05: Lowercase the text and remove the punctuation marks before splitting it into words.
Splitting on a space leaves empty strings where there were several spaces in a row. Skip them.
For each word, add 1 to its count in the object, starting from 0 when the word is new.
ex06: Handle the empty list first, before any calculation.
Math.min and Math.max accept several numbers: spread the array into them.
The trend only depends on the first and the last reading.
ex07: Check each rule separately, in the order listed, and add the rule's name to the result when it fails.
A regular expression like /[A-Z]/ tests whether a string contains at least one character in that range.
Each rule is an independent `if`, not an `else if`: one password can break several rules.
ex08: Handle one character at a time: is it a lowercase letter, an uppercase letter, or something else?
Turn the letter into its position in the alphabet (0 to 25) by subtracting the code of 'a' or 'A', shift it, then convert back.
To wrap around, use the remainder by 26. For negative shifts, add 26 and take the remainder again so the position is never negative.
ex09: To encode, walk through the text keeping a count of how many times the current character has repeated.
When the next character is different (or the text ends), write the count and the character, then reset the count.
To decode, collect digits into a string until you find a letter, then repeat that letter Number(digits) times.
ex10: For toRoman, list every symbol with its value, including the subtractive pairs like CM and IV, from largest to smallest.
While the number is at least the current value, add the symbol and subtract the value.
For fromRoman, a symbol is subtracted when the next symbol has a bigger value. Otherwise it is added.
ex11: There are only 8 ways to win: 3 rows, 3 columns and 2 diagonals. You can list them all.
A line is a win when its three cells are equal and not empty.
If no line wins, the game is a draw when no cell is empty, and still going otherwise.
ex12: In the transposed matrix, the value at row r, column c comes from row c, column r of the original.
The new matrix has as many rows as the original has columns.
Rotating clockwise is the same as transposing and then reversing each row.
ex13: Walk through the array. Values that aren't arrays go straight into the result.
When a value is an array, flatten it first by calling your own function, then add all of its values to the result.
The recursion stops by itself: an array with no arrays inside never calls the function again.
ex14: Anagrams have the same letters, so sorting the letters gives them all the same key.
Use an object to collect the words of each group under their key.
Object keys that are strings keep the order in which they were first added, so the groups come out in the right order.
ex15: Sort a copy of the array, not the original one.
The comparison function sorts by score first. Only when the scores are equal does it compare the names.
After sorting, map each player to a string. The position is the index plus one.
ex16: Write and test the functions in order: each one can use the ones before it.
report only needs to call average and letterGrade for each student.
For bestStudent, keep the best entry so far and replace it only when you find a strictly higher average.
ex17: Three steps: keep only the items below their minimum, sort them by name, turn each one into a string.
The amount to order is twice the minimum minus what's already in stock.
localeCompare is a convenient way to compare strings in a sort.
ex18: Because multiplication comes first, the expression is a sum of products: split it on ' + ' first.
Each piece of the sum is a product: split it on ' * ' and multiply the numbers.
Validate every number before using it: it must be made only of digits. Empty pieces and other symbols are invalid.
ex19: Declare the balance and the history as variables inside createAccount, before the returned object.
Check every rule before changing anything, so a failed operation leaves the account untouched.
history() should return a new array with new objects, so changes from outside don't reach the account.
ex20: Keep the items in an object, keyed by name, with the price and the quantity of each one.
Store the discount as a rate (like 0.1) and apply it only when calculating the total.
Validate the discount code before changing the current discount, so an invalid code doesn't affect the cart.
